lesson.title: Filling space

lead.text: Start with the layer you can see when the lid comes off. The cubes sit in rows, and every row holds the same number. If a row has 6 cubes and the layer has 3 rows, the layer holds 3 × 6 = 18 cubes, which is quicker to find than counting each one.

Under that layer sits another exactly like it, and under that another. If the box is two layers deep, it holds twice as many cubes as one layer, so 2 × 18 = 36. A box four layers deep would hold 4 × 18 = 72. Each new layer adds the same number again, which is why multiplying works.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two boxes. The layer is the same size in both, and only the number of layers changes. To find the cubes in a box, multiply the cubes in a row by the number of rows, then multiply by the number of layers. A cube that is exactly 1 cm along every edge is called a unit cube, and the boxes in this lesson are all measured in them.

lead.text: Use the layers-and-rows method on a real box. Find how many cubes make one layer first.

The number of unit cubes that fill a space is called its volume, so the box with two layers of 18 cubes has a volume of 36 unit cubes. If each unit cube is 1 cm along every edge, the volume is given in cubic centimetres. Here that is 36 cubic centimetres, written 36 cm³.

The unit follows from how many directions you measure in. A length goes in one direction and is measured in centimetres. An area covers a flat surface with squares 1 cm by 1 cm, so it is measured in square centimetres, cm². Volume fills space with cubes 1 cm by 1 cm by 1 cm, and each cube reaches along, across and up. That third direction is why the small raised 3 appears.
Bigger spaces use bigger units in the same way. A room might have a volume of 40 cubic metres, written 40 m³, which is 40 cubes with edges 1 m long.
Think about how many directions you need to measure in to fill a box.

You don't have to build a box out of cubes to count them, because its three measurements tell you everything. Take a box 9 cm long, 2 cm wide and 3 cm high. Rows of 9 cubes run along its length, and 2 of those rows fit across its width, so the bottom layer holds 9 × 2 = 18 cubes. That number is also the area of the base in square centimetres, because each cube stands on a 1 cm by 1 cm square of the floor.

The height says how many layers there are. A height of 3 cm means 3 layers, so the box holds 18 × 3 = 54 cubes, a volume of 54 cm³. As a rule, volume = base area × height, and since the base area is length × width, that is length × width × height.

afterFigure.text: The second drawing is the same box stood on its end. Its base is 3 by 2, which holds 6 cubes, and there are 9 layers, so 6 × 9 = 54 again. Any face can be the base, because multiplying three numbers gives the same answer in whatever order you take them.

lead.text: This box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. Picture one layer of unit cubes, then the layers stacked on it.

reveal.text: You counted one layer of 4 × 3 and stacked two of them. Length × width × height counts every cube once.

steps.headline: A box is 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 4 cm high. Find its volume.

workedSteps.text: Find the cubes in one layer.

steps.headline: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 5 cm high. Find its volume.

workedSteps.text: Find the cubes in one layer.

lead.text: So far you have been given the box and asked for its volume. Sometimes it goes the other way: you know how much a box holds and one measurement is missing. The multiplication can be run backwards. Take a box that holds 96 cm³ with a base 8 cm by 3 cm, and suppose its height is the missing piece.
Each layer holds 8 × 3 = 24 cubes, so the question is how many layers of 24 cubes make 96. Fitting equal groups into a total is division: 96 ÷ 24 = 4. The box has 4 layers, so it is 4 cm high.

afterFigure.text: Check by multiplying forwards: 24 × 4 = 96, the volume you started with. Divide the volume by the base area to get the height, and multiply the base area by the height to get the volume back. Each step undoes the other.

lead.text: The box has a volume, a length and a width. Work out how many cubes fit in one layer, then how many layers make the total.

A cube is a box whose length, width and height are all equal, so one number, its side, describes it. Take a cube with sides 3 cm. Its bottom layer is 3 × 3 = 9 cubes and there are 3 layers, so its volume is 9 × 3 = 27 cm³. In short that is side × side × side, written 3³ and read as three cubed.

Cubes of different sizes show how quickly the volume grows. A cube with side 1 cm holds 1 cm³, and one with side 2 cm holds 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. Doubling the side makes room for eight times as many unit cubes, because the layer grows in two directions and the number of layers grows as well.

afterFigure.text: For a cube with side s, the volume is s × s × s, whatever the size.

lead.text: A cube has three equal edges. Use its side in all three places.

lesson.orientation: Count volume in cubic units, then work back from a volume to a missing height.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A café keeps its sugar in flat cardboard boxes packed with sugar cubes, and every cube is exactly 1 cm along each edge. Lift the lid and you can see the top layer: neat rows of white squares with no gaps between them. Underneath there are more layers packed the same way, but you can't see them.

The person who orders the supplies wants to know how many sugar cubes a box holds. Taking them all out to count would take ages and would spoil the packing, so a better way is needed, one that uses only the box itself. Its length, its width and its height are all you can measure from outside.

In the last lesson every shape was flat, and one number, its area, said how much surface it covered. A box has depth as well as length and width, so it needs a new kind of measurement. This lesson shows how to count what fits inside a box from those three measurements.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out what a box holds from its three measurements, and its height from what it holds.

recap.keyIdea: Volume is length × width × height, in cubic units. Divide by the base area to find a missing height.

blocks.text: You counted 30 cubes in 3 layers of 10, and learned that the count is called volume, measured in cubic units.
You also found 60 cm³ for a box 4 by 3 by 5 and 216 cm³ for a cube with sides of 6 cm. Working back from 120 cm³ gave a height of 5 cm.

recap.nextHook: A box has an outside as well as an inside. A present in a box needs wrapping paper over every face, and the next lesson unfolds a box flat to measure how much.

questions.prompt: A rectangular box has inside dimensions 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: Find the number of unit cubes in one layer.
Multiply by the number of layers.
Calculate 4 × 3 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each layer holds 4 × 3 = 12 unit cubes; two layers give 24 cm³.

questions.onCorrect: 24 cm³. One layer of 4 × 3, repeated for 2 layers.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is one layer. The box is two layers high.
That adds 4 + 3 + 2. Volume multiplies the three lengths.

questions.prompt: A box has inside dimensions 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: Use the base area and height.
The 4 by 3 base is repeated through five layers.
Calculate 4 × 3 × 5.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is one layer. The box is five layers high.

questions.prompt: Which unit measures how much space is inside a box?
hints: Count the independent dimensions needed to fill the box.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Volume counts three-dimensional unit cubes, so it uses cubic centimetres.

questions.onCorrect: Cubic centimetres. Volume counts unit cubes, which have length, width and height.

misconceptions.feedback: Centimetres measure a length. Volume counts cubes.
Square centimetres measure a flat surface. Space inside needs a third direction.

questions.prompt: A cube has sides 6 cm long. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: A cube has three equal edge dimensions.
Use the larger side length three times.
Calculate 6³.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The larger cube has volume 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 cm³.

questions.onCorrect: 216 cm³. A cube's volume is side × side × side.

misconceptions.feedback: 36 is the area of one face. Multiply by the side once more.
That adds 6 + 6 + 6. Volume multiplies the three edges.

questions.prompt: A storage box has inside dimensions 8 m by 5 m by 4 m. Find its volume in cubic metres.
hints: First find the base area.
Multiply that area by the height.
Calculate 8 × 5 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 160 m³. Base area 40, times a height of 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three edges. Volume multiplies them.
40 is one layer. Multiply by the height too.

questions.prompt: A rectangular box has volume 120 cm³, length 6 cm and width 4 cm. Find its height in centimetres.
hints: Volume is base area times height. What is the base area?
Find 6 × 4.
Divide 120 by the base area.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Its base area is 6 × 4 = 24 cm²; height = 120/24 = 5 cm.

questions.onCorrect: 5 cm. Volume ÷ base area gives the height.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies all three numbers. Divide the volume by the base area.
That divides by the width only. Divide by the whole base, length × width.

questions.prompt: A box holds sugar cubes in layers. Each layer has 2 rows of 5 cubes, and 3 layers are stacked. How many sugar cubes are in the box?
hints: How many cubes make one layer of 2 rows of 5?
How many layers are stacked?
Multiply the cubes in a layer by the number of layers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One layer is 5 × 2 = 10 cubes. Three layers hold 10 × 3 = 30.

questions.onCorrect: 30. One layer holds 2 × 5 = 10 cubes, and three layers hold three times as many.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one layer. There are three layers.

questions.prompt: Why multiply the layer by the height?
hints: How many layers stack up?

acceptedIdeas: The base layer is repeated once for each unit of height.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The base layer is repeated once for each unit of height.

choices.label: The base layer is repeated once for each unit of height.
Because height is the longest edge.
Because volume is always the base plus the height.

questions.onCorrect: The base layer repeats for every unit of height, so the volume is base × height.

misconceptions.feedback: Height can be any edge. The point is that layers stack.
Adding would not count the stacked layers. Repeated layers multiply.

questions.prompt: A box has inside dimensions 7 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: How many cubes fit in one layer?
How many layers are there?
Multiply the layer by the number of layers.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three edges. Volume multiplies them.
21 is one layer. There are two layers.

questions.prompt: A cube has sides 5 cm long. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: A cube's three edges are equal.
Multiply 5 × 5 first.
Then multiply by 5 again.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three edges. Volume multiplies them.
25 is one face. Multiply by 5 once more.

questions.prompt: A box holds 90 m³. Its base is 10 m by 3 m. How high is it, in metres?
hints: Find the area of the base.
Volume is base area times height.
Divide 90 by the base area.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m. The base area is 30 m², and 90 ÷ 30 = 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 30 is the base area. Divide the volume by it to get the height.
That multiplies. Volume is base × height, so go back by dividing.
